Dermatology · published research

Radiation dermatitis

Several controlled studies, including a 120-person placebo-controlled trial, found fewer moderate-to-severe acute skin reactions with PBM, and pooled analyses favor prevention. Other trials were null or inconclusive, so the size and transferability of benefit depend on setting and protocol.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several controlled studies, including a 120-person placebo-controlled trial, found fewer moderate-to-severe acute skin reactions with PBM, and pooled analyses favor prevention. Other trials were null or inconclusive, so the size and transferability of benefit depend on setting and protocol.

Summary of the Evidence

Thirty-five records address radiation dermatitis: 34 are assigned directly to this category and one is a cross-category long-term follow-up. They include about 17 human primary reports representing roughly 15 cohorts, 12 reviews or guidance publications, four animal studies, and two trial protocols. Three publications report different outcomes from the same 120-person TRANSDERMIS cohort and are not three independent trials. Reviews and meta-analyses also reuse primary cohorts, so their publication counts should not be added to the number of patients studied.

Human and clinical evidence

The placebo-controlled TRANSDERMIS trial randomized 120 women receiving breast radiotherapy, 60 per group. At the end of radiotherapy, grade 2 or worse dermatitis occurred in 30% of placebo participants and 6.7% of those receiving PBM. The trial also reported better patient-reported skin symptoms and quality-of-life measures (Robijns et al. 2018). A later report and long-term follow-up use the same cohort. At a median follow-up of 66 months, the follow-up publication found no adverse signal for cancer recurrence or survival; it is useful safety information but not another prevention trial (Robijns et al. 2022).

The DERMISHEAD randomized trial in head-and-neck radiotherapy also reported a reduction in acute dermatitis severity (Robijns et al. 2021). In the 71-person LABRA trial, severe reactions were numerically less frequent with PBM, 10% versus 28%, but the primary comparison did not reach statistical significance (Robijns et al. 2021). A smaller blinded study using yellow light did not find a clear preventive effect (Fife et al., 2010). Thus, some controlled trials show meaningful reductions, while the effect is not uniform across settings.

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling five randomized-trial reports favored PBM for prevention of more severe acute reactions; the pooled result should be interpreted alongside the small number of trials and shared cohorts (Gobbo et al. 2023).

Animal evidence

Four mouse or rat studies reported lower dermatitis severity or inflammation and improved healing after PBM. These findings support biological activity in irradiated skin models but do not replace the clinical radiotherapy trials.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No indication-specific in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

TRANSDERMIS used a class-IV device delivering 808–905-nm near-infrared light at 4 J/cm² twice weekly during radiotherapy. Other studies used different near-infrared or red protocols, while some tested 590-nm amber-yellow visible light. Treatment site, cancer therapy, timing, device, and dermatitis grading differ. No single wavelength or schedule has been shown superior in a direct comparison. The favorable results are most applicable to the cancer sites and radiotherapy regimens actually studied.

Interpretation

The strongest trial evidence shows fewer grade 2 or worse reactions in one breast-radiotherapy cohort, and a head-and-neck trial and pooled randomized evidence also favor PBM. A null trial and an inconclusive comparison show that benefit is not automatic across protocols. Taken together, the findings support a probable preventive benefit in some radiotherapy settings, with further independent trials needed to define where and how consistently it occurs.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for reducing grade 2 or worse acute dermatitis in selected radiotherapy settings Low for symptom and quality-of-life effects across settings
Publications and records35 articles (34 direct-category; 1 long-term follow-up mapped)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A placebo-controlled trial of 120 breast-cancer patients found fewer moderate-or-worse reactions, and a head-and-neck trial and pooled analyses also favor PBM. The results are not uniform: one trial was null and the LABRA comparison narrowly missed statistical significance. Further independent, adequately powered trials using common severity and patient-reported outcomes would clarify which cancer sites and schedules benefit most.
